title: Feature Flags and Kill Switches
intro: Big companies separate deploying code from releasing features. Code ships 'dark' behind a flag, and turning the feature on or off is a configuration change: instant, targeted, and reversible without a deploy. A kill switch is a flag whose job is to switch off something expensive or broken during an incident.

steps.prompt: The new recommendations widget is overloading the database. Check the flag service's current state for the flag reco-widget: GET http://flags.internal/flags/reco-widget.
steps.why: When a problem starts right after a flag flips, the flag is as good a suspect as a deploy. Flag changes must be audited (who, when) exactly like deploys, and shown in the same timeline.

steps.prompt: Turn it off: PATCH the flag to enabled=false.
steps.explanation: The widget disappears for all users within seconds; database load drops.
steps.why: Mitigation in seconds with no deploy, no rollback of unrelated changes in the same release, and it's reversible. That's why risky features ship behind flags. Dedicated tools (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature-compatible services) add targeting, percentage rollouts, and audit logs.

steps.prompt: A simpler service reads a kill switch from an environment variable: set PDF_EXPORT_ENABLED=false on deployment reports in namespace shop.
expected_commands: kubectl set env deployment/reports PDF_EXPORT_ENABLED=false -n shop
kubectl set env deploy/reports PDF_EXPORT_ENABLED=false -n shop
steps.explanation: A new rollout starts with PDF export disabled.
steps.why: Environment-variable switches work everywhere, but they need a rollout (a restart), taking minutes rather than seconds. That's fine for a kill switch, too slow for gradual rollouts. Know which kind each of your switches is before the incident.

steps.prompt: The flag config for the storefront lives in a ConfigMap. Check the current values of storefront-flags in shop.
expected_commands: kubectl get configmap storefront-flags -n shop -o yaml
kubectl get cm storefront-flags -n shop -o yaml
steps.explanation: The new checkout flow is at 25% of users.
steps.why: Percentage rollouts are canaries at the feature level: 1%, then 5%, 25%, 100%, watching metrics at each step. Clean up flags once a feature is at 100%: stale flags are dead code paths, and a well-known outage at Knight Capital involved an old flag reused for new behaviour.

steps.prompt: The app reads the ConfigMap only at startup. Restart deployment storefront in shop so it picks up the change.
steps.explanation: A rolling restart loads the new flag values.
steps.why: ConfigMaps mounted as files update in place after a short delay, but environment variables built from them never do, and many apps only read config at startup anyway. A rolling restart is the reliable way to apply a change, and it respects the deployment's surge and availability settings.
